content: The International Health Regulations (IHR) (2005) Assessment Tool for Core Capacity Requirements at Designated Airports, Ports, and Ground Crossings, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2009, is a comprehensive guide designed to assist countries in evaluating and strengthening their public health capacities at points of entry. This tool aligns with the IHR (2005), a legally binding international framework adopted in May 2005 and enforced from June 15, 2007, to enhance global collaboration in preventing and responding to the international spread of diseases while minimizing disruptions to international travel and trade. The document emphasizes that the designations and content presented do not imply any legal or political stance by WHO regarding the status of countries, territories, or boundaries. It also clarifies that references to specific companies or products do not constitute endorsements. WHO has taken all reasonable precautions to verify the information provided, but the responsibility for its interpretation and use lies with the reader. The IHR (2005) requires countries to develop, strengthen, and maintain core public health capacities to detect, assess, notify, and respond to public health risks and emergencies of international concern (PHEIC). The assessment tool is structured into two main parts: 1. Part A: Focuses on evaluating the establishment of communication and collaboration structures between competent authorities at points of entry and national, intermediate, and local health authorities, as outlined in Annex 1A of the IHR. 2. Part B: Provides a checklist for assessing core capacity requirements at designated airports, ports, and ground crossings, as per Annex 1B of the IHR. The IHR (2005) obligates countries to designate international airports, ports, and, where justified, ground crossings to minimize the risk of disease spread through transportation, travel, and trade. Competent authorities are required to conduct inspections, supervise service providers, and implement vector control programs. The document highlights the importance of international and national communication links between competent authorities at points of entry and health authorities at all levels. It also stresses the need for contingency plans to address unexpected public health events and the integration of IHR requirements into existing national plans, such as pandemic preparedness plans. Monitoring the implementation of IHR core capacities began on June 15, 2009, with a target for countries to achieve minimum capacities by 2012. WHO provides monitoring tools, including an Excel spreadsheet model and a checklist, to facilitate the assessment and tracking of progress. In summary, the IHR (2005) Assessment Tool serves as a critical resource for countries to evaluate and enhance their public health capacities at points of entry, ensuring effective prevention, detection, and response to public health risks and emergencies while supporting global health security.
